title: Uniform exact permanent circuits below base two
formal:
Does there exist a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and one deterministic circuit generator \(G\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), \(G(1^{n})\) outputs a division-free rational arithmetic circuit \(\mathcal C_{n}\) with at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) nodes, within at most \(C(2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) Turing-machine steps, and
\[\forall K\text{ of characteristic zero}\ \forall A\in K^{n\times n},\qquad \mathcal C_{n}(A)=\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
Here \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), and every rational circuit constant is interpreted through the canonical embedding \(\mathbb Q\to K\). This fixes the uniform rational-circuit version of the saved characteristic-zero arithmetic-operation question.
why: A canonical exponential-time algebraic computation barrier dating to Ryser's formula.

sentences: The permanent is the unsigned sum of permutation products of a square matrix.
This card asks whether exact division-free rational circuits can beat exponential base two while being generated uniformly within the same exponential bound.
The generated polynomial must work for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field, with bit costs for circuit construction separated from field-operation costs for evaluation.
Checked recent results give conditional circuit improvements, finite-ring algorithms, bounded-entry bit-time savings or lower bounds for restricted formula classes.
A complete Lean proof must establish the specified uniform circuit family with a fixed positive base saving or rule out every family meeting these conventions.

definitions:
A field \(K\) has characteristic zero when the sum of any positive number of copies of its multiplicative identity is nonzero; this gives a unique injective field homomorphism \(\mathbb Q\to K\). The domain contains every square matrix over every such field, including rational, real and complex matrices, with no sign, magnitude, sparsity, rank, symmetry or integrality promise. The permanent is the unsigned permutation sum above; it is not the determinant. All evaluations must be exact.

An arithmetic circuit is a finite list of nodes in topological order, with the last node the output. Each node is either an input variable \(x_{i,j}\) with \(0\le i,j<n\), a rational constant, or a binary \(+\), \(-\), or \(\times\) gate whose two ordered parent indices refer to earlier nodes. Repeated use of the same parent is allowed, so shared intermediate values and squaring are permitted. Unused nodes may be omitted. The size counts all nodes, including constants and variable nodes. On a matrix \(A\), an input node evaluates to its entry, constants are embedded in \(K\), and internal gates perform the indicated field operations. Each internal gate costs one arithmetic operation, independently of the sizes of field elements; a rational constant is a permitted circuit input. There is no division by an input-dependent value, branching on an input entry, rounding, bit extraction, transcendental gate, oracle gate, or limit computation. Subtraction is equivalently addition using the constant \(-1\), so it does not introduce an extra algebraic operation type beyond the source circuit convention.

The generator is one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine over fixed finite alphabets, given only \(1^{n}\). It receives neither matrix entries nor a description of the field. Its program and clock constants are fixed independently of \(n\). For definiteness, for a nonnegative integer \(t\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion with \(b(0)=0\), and encode \(t\) by \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). The output begins with the encoded positive node count. Each node then has a three-bit tag: 000 for a variable followed by \(E(i)E(j)\); 001 for a constant followed by a sign bit and \(E(u)E(v)\), representing \((-1)^{s}u/v\), with \(u\ge0,v\ge1\) in lowest terms and zero having sign zero; 010, 011 or 100 for addition, subtraction or multiplication followed by the two encoded parent indices. Indices start at zero, and the output must be a well-formed list with no trailing bits. Every generator transition, including writing every constant and index bit, is charged. Thus a separate unbounded search or arbitrary nonuniform circuit choice is not hidden outside the construction bound.

Circuit generation and field evaluation are different costs: the first is bounded binary computation on the dimension, while the second counts exact field operations on abstract entries. There is no claim of a bit-time bound independent of entry length when evaluating on encoded integers or rationals. The same generated rational polynomial must work in all characteristic-zero fields; no field-dependent or noncomputable constants are allowed. This is a specified uniform circuit model, not an assertion that all branching arithmetic algorithms or all field-specific circuit models are equivalent to it. The fixed base saving is uniform in dimension. Polynomial prefactors may be absorbed by a smaller positive base saving, but \(2^{n-o(n)}\) alone does not meet the target. This is an exact complexity-existence question, so absolute numerical tolerance does not apply.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite generator, rational \(\varepsilon\), integer \(C\), valid output circuits and their two bounds for every dimension, and prove their exact evaluation identity for every matrix over every characteristic-zero field. A polynomial identity proof over \(\mathbb Q\), together with its transfer under the canonical field embedding, can establish the required universal identity. A negative answer must exclude every permitted generator and every fixed positive base saving, rather than one construction, bounded circuit depth or coefficient pattern. It need not be a single finite counterexample matrix. A conditional implication is only conditional unless its hypotheses are also proved. Approximate permanent values, algorithms only for bounded integer entries or finite rings, a sublinear saving in the exponent, and small circuits with no generator meeting the bound do not suffice. A negative result for this precise circuit model is not automatically a lower bound for every stronger arithmetic model.

context_blocks.text: Ryser’s classical upper bound uses \(O(n2^{n})\) field operations to compute the permanent. A fixed improvement from exponential base two would change the scale of exact algebraic counting, while still allowing exponential running time. Exact #P-completeness on zero–one integer matrices explains the absence of an expected polynomial-time counting algorithm, but it does not rule out a fixed exponential-base improvement in this arithmetic model.

For a \(2\times2\) matrix with rows \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), the permanent is \(ad+bc\), whereas the determinant is \(ad-bc\). Removing alternating signs changes the algebraic complexity substantially. On nonnegative entries the permanent also counts weighted bipartite perfect matchings, but this card allows every field entry and asks for exact evaluation. The randomized or deterministic relative approximations in the neighboring cards do not give this circuit family.

The proposal cited the uniform-circuit results of Björklund, Kaski, Koana and Nederlof. Their Section 2.2 uses division-free arithmetic circuits, and Theorem 1.3 bounds both construction time and circuit size. This card makes the previously unstated coefficient and uniformity conventions concrete by choosing a finite generator of rational circuits that works throughout characteristic zero. This portable rational model and the fixed exponential-base target are explicit editorial choices; they are not presented as identical to every possible reading of Knuth’s broader arithmetic-operation question quoted in that source.

The ICALP 2026 paper proves that a sufficiently low rank growth rate for a sequence of balanced tripartitioning tensors yields a uniform permanent circuit construction with a fixed exponential improvement. It relates the needed rank bounds to Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture. A tensor rank here is the least number of products of three linear forms needed to express the associated trilinear form. These are conditional upper bounds with a specified underlying field; the paper does not establish the required rank hypothesis unconditionally or identify every coefficient model. Its result is relevant evidence about the barrier, not a completed positive answer.

Björklund and Williams give a deterministic \(2^{n-\Omega(n/r)}\)-time permanent algorithm over a finite ring with \(r\le n\) elements. For fixed \(r\) this is a fixed base improvement, but a finite field has positive characteristic and is outside this card’s domain. They also obtain faster exact counting on regular zero–one matrices, where the saving depends on the degree. Those input restrictions must be retained when comparing the theorem to an unrestricted characteristic-zero circuit family.

Baitian Li’s revised paper of 3 May 2026, published at ICALP 2026, gives \(2^{n-\Omega(\sqrt n)}\)-type bit-time bounds for integer permanents, with polynomial dependence on the bit bound for entries. Its hafnian formulation uses a \(2n\times2n\) symmetric matrix; a permanent of order \(n\) is a special case at that size. The theorem is a significant exact speedup, but its sublinear exponent saving is not a fixed \((2-\varepsilon)^{n}\) guarantee, and its numerical operations are not this input-oblivious characteristic-zero circuit model. The revised title and more general hafnian scope replace the older title in the proposal’s reference trail.

Fonollosa’s July 2026 preprint compares Ryser, Glynn and Fourier evaluation formulas at the same \(\Theta(n2^{n})\) arithmetic scale. Its revised Corollary 1 gives a lower bound on the number of evaluations for the particular row-product evaluation schemes considered in that paper. That restricted-formula bound does not rule out general arithmetic circuits with reused intermediate values and unrestricted depth. The new proof was not independently verified in full during this review.

The fixed base, the dimension, the field, the coefficient representation and uniform construction all matter. A finite-ring computation, an experiment on structured matrices, a smaller constant number of exponential terms or a better approximate count may be useful without answering this question. A resolution would clarify the exact algebraic cost of one of the central counting polynomials.
